extracted.intended_audience: NIH/NIAID grant applicants whose applications were not funded (principal investigators and research teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for investigators on how to assess reviewer feedback (summary statement and program officer input), determine whether problems are fixable, and choose among revising/resubmitting, submitting a new application, applying outside NIH, or appealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your Summary Statement to assess fixability and reviewer appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your summary statement carefully and analytically to gain insight into two questions: Are the application's problems fixable? Was it reviewed by the right study section?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the summary statement to colleagues for their interpretation. To assess the type of criticism you got, ask: Did the reviewers think the topic was significant? Did they identify fixable problems? Did they misunderstand some points that you could easily clarify? Did they have major conceptual issues (e.g., research not state-of-the-art, experiments won't prove the hypothesis)? Did they seem to be the right reviewers? Also be aware of limitations: low enthusiasm or a 'fatal flaw' noted may mean no amount of revising helps; reviewers may stop discussion and feedback may be incomplete; a resubmission may face different reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult your Program Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact your program officer after reviewing your summary statement for interpretation and to learn about funding prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about chances of special funding (some applications above the payline receive special actions). If on a special funding list, revise and resubmit promptly. Program officers (who may attend review meetings as observers) can help interpret the level of enthusiasm and advise on next steps. Also seek input from senior colleagues, mentors, and institutional investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Were they the right reviewers? (Reviewer expertise fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the study section reviewers' expertise matched your topic and methods and whether they understood your rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Did the reviewers' expertise fit your topic? Were they knowledgeable about your methods? Did they understand the rationale for your research? Check the roster attached to your summary statement and get input from colleagues and your program officer. If misassigned, consider requesting a different study section for a resubmission, but remember that often the problem is the application, not the reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether it's worth fixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether you can resolve the problems identified and whether reviewers showed sufficient interest to merit revising and resubmitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have brutally honest colleagues, students, and your program officer gauge reviewer interest and whether issues are resolvable. Many fixable critiques may indicate reviewer interest and be a good sign. Conversely, faint praise (no major criticisms but poor outcome) often signals lack of excitement and suggests revising won't help. If reviewers found deal-breaking flaws (e.g., unexciting topic) revising is unlikely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined (not discussed) application considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that streamlined applications (not discussed) don't get a full review, making it harder to assess reviewers' appraisals and decide on next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlining may result from a crowded pool or many outstanding applications. Your application may still be worth revising. Use the reviewer critiques to identify problem areas and follow the guidance on fixing issues or choosing other strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixable problem: Poor writing, formatting, or presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers identify issues with writing, formatting, or presentation, these are generally fixable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite; get help with writing, editing, formatting, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixable problem: Insufficient information, experimental details, or preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of necessary experimental detail or preliminary data is a common, addressable defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess what's missing and add it to the Research Plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixable problem: Significance not convincingly stated
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers are unconvinced of the study's significance, that can be remedied by clarifying importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beef up the Significance section; explicitly show the importance to NIAID's mission, your scientific area, and public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixable problem: Research feasibility not demonstrated by proposed staff
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers doubt that the proposed team can carry out the work, this is fixable by adjusting personnel or collaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit collaborators and consultants with the required expertise onto your project; document team qualifications more convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixable problem: Insufficient discussion of obstacles and alternative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to describe potential pitfalls and alternatives is a correctable weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe contingency plans for negative results and alternative approaches. Include decision trees where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-to-fix problem: Low-impact research topic
rubrics_metrics.description: If the research topic is judged to be low impact, this is inherently difficult or impossible to fix through revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider starting over with a new topic rather than investing in revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-to-fix problem: Philosophical issues (reviewers don't think the work is important)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers fundamentally disagree about the importance or philosophical approach of the project, it is seldom fixable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this is the barrier, plan a new direction; consult mentors and program officers, but revising is unlikely to overcome this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-to-fix problem: Unsound or unsupported hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis that is not sound or not supported by data is a near-impossible flaw to correct by revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandon or substantially redesign the project; develop stronger preliminary data or a new hypothesis before resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-to-fix problem: Work has already been done
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed work has already been performed or is not novel, this is not fixable by revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a new research question or demonstrate clear novelty with new data or angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-to-fix problem: Methods not suitable for testing the hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed methods are fundamentally inappropriate for the hypothesis, this is very difficult to remedy by revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redesign the approach or propose different methods; if the mismatch is irreparable, consider a new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance review criterion—take poor scores seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor scores on the Significance or Importance review criterion indicate reviewers aren't excited about the research and merit special attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk to your program officer before preparing another application. Continuing the same line of research when significance is lacking is unlikely to lead to funding; avoid pouring time into an un-fundable idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision strategies after non-funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on whether problems are fixable and program officer input, choose among revising/resubmitting, creating a new application, or seeking funding outside NIH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fixable problems: Revise and resubmit. If problems aren't fixable or you've exhausted resubmission opportunities: create a new application (similar idea or new topic) or apply to non-NIH funders. Consult your program officer to decide which strategy suits the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals of Scientific Review—when and how (and why generally not to appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may have grounds to appeal in certain circumstances, but appeals are not for differences of scientific opinion and are generally not recommended as a path to funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the SOP on Appeals of Scientific Review for specifics. Most appeals are denied; if upheld, your original application is re-reviewed (you cannot revise it before re-review and you usually wait another review round). Appeals seldom improve chances of eventual funding; usually better to revise and resubmit or submit a new application.
